problem: This review asks where quantum machine learning (QML) could realistically help data analysis, with emphasis on quantum data from materials science, biochemistry and high-energy physics.
gap: Early enthusiasm paid less attention to whether these models can actually be trained and how they truly differ from classical learning.
method: The authors survey current methods and applications, giving most attention to quantum neural and deep learning models, and contrast them with classical machine learning.
results: As a review it reports no new experiments. Its main message is that trainability remains an open obstacle, while quantum data is named as an especially promising setting.
limits: The focus on quantum data leaves classical tabular problems, such as medical diagnosis, less directly addressed, so its conclusions need testing on those datasets.
mm: Survey of QNNs and quantum deep learning
f: Trainability is the central open challenge; quantum data looks most promising
l: No new experiments; little on classical tabular data

problem: This perspective questions whether proving quantum advantage should be the main goal of QML research.
gap: Classical machine learning works well in practice but is hard to analyse, whereas quantum computing cannot yet be tested at realistic scale. Judging practical quantum power is therefore unusually difficult, yet the literature often assumes a race against classical models.
method: The authors reason through why the available tools struggle to answer this question, and they point to existing work that takes other viewpoints.
results: They call for a critical debate on the narrative of beating classical models and argue that other research perspectives are an important alternative. No numerical results are presented.
limits: Being an opinion-based perspective, it gives direction rather than evidence. Its advice still has to be applied through careful, honest studies on real data.
f: Questions the focus on beating classical ML; proposes other research goals
l: No experiments; gives direction, not evidence

problem: This paper asks when a quantum model can really outperform classical learners once training data is available.
gap: Most complexity arguments consider computation without data, yet data can make a classically hard function easy to predict.
method: The authors derive prediction-error bounds and use them as a test for potential advantage. They also propose a projected quantum kernel model and run numerical tests with up to 30 qubits.
results: With data, classical models were often competitive even on problems tailored to quantum models. The projected model gave a rigorous speed-up in the fault-tolerant setting and a clear near-term advantage on engineered datasets.
limits: The near-term advantage was shown on datasets deliberately built to favour quantum models, so it does not automatically carry over to real-world data such as clinical records.
mm: Theory plus simulations up to 30 qubits on engineered data
f: Data lets classical models compete; projected kernel gives advantage on engineered data
l: Advantage shown on data built to favour quantum models

problem: This work seeks a provable quantum speed-up for supervised classification that needs only classical access to the data.
gap: Earlier algorithms either assumed quantum access to data or were heuristics with no proof of advantage.
method: A conventional support vector machine (SVM) is combined with a fault-tolerant quantum computer that estimates the kernel as a circuit transition amplitude. The authors construct a family of datasets linked to the discrete logarithm problem.
results: Assuming that problem is hard, no classical learner beats random guessing by more than an inverse polynomial, while the quantum classifier reaches high accuracy and tolerates additive kernel errors from finite sampling.
limits: The proof depends on fault-tolerant hardware and artificially constructed data. It therefore says little about near-term devices or about natural datasets.
f: Rigorous speed-up with classical data access; robust to sampling error
l: Needs fault tolerance; constructed data only

problem: This study examines how well variational QML models generalise after training on only a limited number of examples.
gap: It was not clearly known how much training data such models need, a key point for applications where data is scarce.
method: The authors prove generalisation bounds in terms of the number of trainable gates T, the number of substantially changed gates K, and the number of training points N.
results: The error grows at worst as the square root of T/N and improves to the square root of K/N when few gates change greatly. Unitary compiling and classifying quantum phases with a quantum convolutional network need little data.
limits: A small generalisation gap does not ensure a low training error or a useful model, and the highlighted applications involve quantum rather than classical data.
mm: Theoretical proofs with QCNN and compiling examples
f: Error scales at worst as sqrt(T/N), improving to sqrt(K/N)
l: Does not ensure low training error; applications use quantum data

problem: This preprint tests how far published claims about QML models hold when they are compared systematically with classical baselines.
gap: Experimental design choices, small scales and commercial narratives make simulated benchmarks hard to interpret reliably.
method: The authors built an open-source PennyLane package and tested 12 popular models on 6 binary classification tasks, forming 160 datasets.
results: Out-of-the-box classical models generally beat the quantum classifiers. Removing entanglement often gave equal or better performance, which hints that quantum effects may not be what matters most at these small scales. Five questions for model design are also identified.
limits: The findings apply to the small tasks that can be simulated today and cannot rule out benefits at larger scale. It was also consulted as a preprint.
f: Classical models outperform; removing entanglement often does not hurt

problem: This foundational paper explores using a quantum state space as the feature space for supervised classification.
gap: Kernel methods become limited when feature spaces grow large and kernels become expensive to compute classically.
method: Two approaches were proposed and run on a superconducting processor: a quantum variational classifier, and a quantum kernel estimator whose output trains a classical SVM.
results: Both algorithms were demonstrated experimentally and solved the construction of a classifier. The work presents feature spaces reachable efficiently only on a quantum computer as a possible route to advantage, and it supplies tools for near-term devices.
limits: The advantage is described only as a possible path, not a proven gain. Real-world performance was left open, which motivates tests on data such as breast cancer records.
f: Quantum feature spaces demonstrated in both methods
l: Advantage remains only a possible path; real data untested

problem: This paper studies the measurement resources needed to estimate quantum kernel values accurately enough for learning.
gap: The convex training of kernel models is attractive, but it assumes that kernel values can be obtained efficiently from hardware.
method: The authors derive analytical concentration bounds for four sources and check them with numerical simulations on several QML tasks.
results: Kernel values for different inputs can concentrate exponentially around a fixed value as qubits increase. With polynomially many measurements, predictions then become independent of the input. Embedding expressivity, global measurements, entanglement and noise are all causes, and kernel alignment can suffer too.
limits: The bounds hold under certain conditions, and they warn about what to avoid rather than offering a complete design recipe for useful kernels.
f: Expressivity, global measurement, entanglement and noise cause concentration
l: Holds under conditions; no full design recipe

problem: This paper seeks a common framework for comparing QML models built from parametrised circuits.
gap: Understanding of how these model families relate to each other and to classical models was still limited.
method: Using quantum information tools, the authors show that all standard models, including data re-uploading circuits, can be mapped to linear models in Hilbert space. They then analyse the qubit and data requirements.
results: For certain learning tasks, linear models need exponentially more qubits than re-uploading models, and kernel methods additionally need exponentially more data points. This separates the models by their resource demands under near-term constraints.
limits: The separations are proven for particular tasks, so they do not indicate which model will work best on a given practical dataset. Empirical comparison remains necessary.
f: Kernels may need exponentially more data than re-uploading models on some tasks
l: Proven for particular tasks; empirical tests still needed

problem: This work addresses how to choose a suitable quantum kernel and how noise affects it on near-term hardware.
gap: Kernel methods face three issues: quadratic cost in training samples, difficult kernel selection, and unknown noise effects. The authors tackle the last two.
method: They introduce trainable quantum embedding kernels tuned through kernel-target alignment. Device and finite-sampling noise are studied, and mitigation methods are compared numerically and on data from a real processor.
results: Training reduced the training error significantly in the tested setup, and the best mitigation strategy raised the quality of the kernel matrix.
limits: The quadratic cost of building the kernel matrix was explicitly left unsolved, and the abstract reports its gains for one experimental setup, without numerical values.
mm: Kernel-target alignment; simulation and real QPU data
f: Training lowers training error; mitigation improves kernel matrix
l: Quadratic cost unsolved; results tied to one setup
